payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=psychological+markers+of+body+signal+outsourcing+and+cognitive+offloading+in+general+populations+using+AI+health+trackers&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.61113/impact.v2i1.1266\", \"title\": [\"Cognitive Offloading in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Psychological Implications of Excessive AI Dependence\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into daily life has transformed how individuals think, learn, decide, and solve problems. While AI technologies offer significant cognitive support by enhancing efficiency and access to information, growing concerns have emerged regarding excessive dependency on AI systems and its potential impact on core cognitive processes. This paper explores how overreliance on AI may influence human cognitive functioning, particularly attention, memory, critical thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making abilities.\\r\\nDrawing on recent empirical studies and theoretical perspectives in cognitive psychology and human–computer interaction, this review examines evidence suggesting that frequent delegation of cognitive tasks to AI tools may contribute to cognitive offloading, reduced mental effort, and diminished engagement of executive functions. Excessive dependency may weaken metacognitive awareness, impair deep information processing, and foster passive learning habits, especially among students and young adults. At the same time, the paper acknowledges that AI can act as a cognitive enhancer when used appropriately, supporting learning, creativity, and adaptive problem-solving.\\r\\nThe paper adopts a narrative review methodology, synthesizing findings from peer-reviewed research published between 2018 and 2025, focusing on AI use in educational, professional, and everyday contexts. Ethical and psychological implications of AI dependency are discussed, emphasizing the need for balanced, human-centered AI use that preserves cognitive autonomy. The study highlights the importance of developing AI literacy, self-regulation skills, and guidelines for responsible AI engagement to prevent cognitive decline while maximizing technological benefits.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.61113/impact.v2i1.1266\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2, 8]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6669899\", \"title\": [\"Cognitive Offloading and the Erosion of Authentic Self-Reflection in AI-Assisted Mental Health Practices\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p><span>Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used in mental health practices, particularly in activities such as journaling and emotional reflection. While these tools improve accessibility and help individuals articulate their thoughts, they also raise concerns about the authenticity of self-reflection. This paper examines how AI-assisted reflection may influence emotional processing through the concept of cognitive offloading, where individuals rely on external systems to perform mental tasks. It argues that while AI can support individuals in organizing their thoughts, over-reliance on these tools may reduce cognitive effort and limit deeper emotional engagement. The paper proposes a conceptual framework suggesting that AI-assisted reflection can lead to reduced effort, which may weaken emotional processing and self-awareness over time. It concludes that AI should function as a support system rather than a replacement for human reflection.</span></p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669899\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780198945215.003.0247\", \"title\": [\"Generative AI and Cognitive Offloading\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>Contemporary generative artificial intelligence software poses a threat to the development of critical thinking skills that sets it apart from the litany of prior technological developments that have raised similar concerns. This article adopts a metacognitive perspective on critical thinking in order to show that AI poses a risk of a critical thinking “death spiral” where AI use degrades critical thinking skill and thereby induces further harmful use. While the evidence on the harmful effects of cognitive offloading on critical thinking is not yet definitive, this article supports the case that AI risks undermining critical thinking abilities by appealing to two lines of evidence. The first is the alignment of features of contemporary AI software with psychological biases that will incline us to trust AI more as our reasoning capacities are degraded. The second draws on social epistemology to show that in the case of expertise identification, consideration of opposing perspectives, and use of evidential “stoppers,” AI undermines social practices and conventions that are constitutive of critical thinking. In light of these considerations, a precautionary principle requires that we do not teach AI skills as part of critical thinking skill development, at least until such time as we have stronger empirical evidence on how to do so without eroding the metacognitive capacity to recognize the right contexts for using rational strategies.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780198945215.003.0247\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 8, 25]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5934297\", \"title\": [\"AI-based cognitive offloading by students in higher education: Factors influencing cognitive delegation to AI\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5934297\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "95589526b020b1133a38874fc4de7ed1831c057c7d248afea777be2021fc3993", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.61113/impact.v2i1.1266", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6669899", "doi:10.1093/9780198945215.003.0247", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.5934297"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.61113/impact.v2i1.1266", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669899", "https://doi.org/10.1093/9780198945215.003.0247", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5934297"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

actions.assumptions_changed: The assumption that automated systems lack any form of rigorous self-correction has been challenged by the existence of automated falsification agents (Popper) and optimized simulation testing.
actions.new_frame: Automated systems can effectively perform hypothesis-level falsification within predefined frameworks, but these mechanisms do not extend to autonomous revision of foundational methodological assumptions.
actions.old_frame: Automated decision-making systems lack external auditing mechanisms for high-stakes tasks.
actions.reason: New evidence demonstrates that while tactical falsification is becoming automated, the foundational assumptions remain exogenous or fixed in the design phase.
actions.strategy: Distinguish between tactical falsification (the 'what' of the data) and strategic epistemic correction (the 'why' of the method).
actions.trigger: Review of Popper and BO evidence.

review.alternative: The system relies on human-defined hypothesis generation and data environments, limiting its 'autonomy'.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of an agent autonomously identifying and correcting a flawed foundational hypothesis generation framework.

claims.statement: Automated falsification agents like Popper can achieve performance comparable to human scientists in validating specific biological hypotheses.

support.explanation: Provides a measured capability for autonomous hypothesis validation against external data.
support.passage: Popper achieved comparable performance in validating complex biological hypotheses while reducing time by 10 folds

review.alternative: Optimization might be misattributed as 'correction' when it is actually 'search' within defined bounds.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of Bayesian optimization discovering that the system model itself was invalid and self-refining it.

claims.statement: Bayesian Optimization enhances falsification efficiency in Cyber-Physical Systems, but relies on predefined system specifications.

support.explanation: Confirms that the system requires exogenous models/specifications to perform falsification.
support.passage: In this paper, we assume the availability of a black-box model representing the system under test (SUT), which can be simulated.

actions.findings:
Automated falsification agents like Popper can achieve performance comparable to human scientists in validating specific biological hypotheses. [source-0c3114b8bfe140df]

Bayesian Optimization enhances falsification efficiency in Cyber-Physical Systems, but relies on predefined system specifications. [source-f0f5479363014d20]
actions.limitations: Existing automated frameworks are highly efficient at testing defined hypotheses but currently lack mechanisms to reflectively challenge their own underlying logic, definitions, or procedural frameworks without external intervention.
actions.next_questions: Can meta-level auditing frameworks be integrated with operational falsification agents to create a hierarchical self-correcting system?
actions.reason: Revision based on new findings regarding Popper and Bayesian Optimization as specific falsification mechanisms distinct from broad epistemic self-correction.
actions.summary: While agentic frameworks like Popper [source-0c3114b8bfe140df] and Bayesian optimization [source-f0f5479363014d20] demonstrate significant advancements in automated hypothesis testing and system falsification, these systems operate within fixed methodological parameters. They do not demonstrate autonomous revision of their foundational epistemic assumptions, which remain subject to the external normative constraints identified in ethics-based auditing literature [source-f26a645e047847a2].
actions.title: Limitations of Automated Epistemic Self-Correction

proposal.summary: This journal entry synthesizes new evidence on automated falsification frameworks (Popper and Bayesian optimization) to refine the project on autonomous epistemic self-correction, distinguishing between task-level hypothesis testing and foundational methodological revision.
proposal.title: Advancing Autonomous Falsification Limits
